item.title: Maine Democrats Have a New Working-Class Hero. Can He Deliver?
item.description:
He rubbed his hands together. He cocked his eyebrows. He gave a little shrug. And as Troy Jackson looked out at hundreds of Democrats cheering his name, he seemed as surprised any anyone to find himself here, in an antiseptic convention center on a hot day, moments away from accepting his party’s nomination for U.S. Senate after the implosion of Graham Platner’s candidacy.

“I went into the woods right after high school — all of us, I was no different,” Jackson said on Saturday, speaking with a gravelly northern accent that swallows some of his words whole. “I’m nothing special.”

Certain aspects of Jackson’s electoral history would support that assessment, politically speaking. A former state legislator, he lost the primary for governor this year, coming in third. He lost the primary when he ran for Congress in 2014. He is not well known outside the State House and the sparsely populated stretches of Northern Maine he represented as a state senator.

But Democrats whom I have spoken to, both in the buzzy hall on Saturday and well beyond, believe that Jackson’s life story makes him very special indeed. They have chosen an honest-to-God lumberjack to finally topple Senator Susan Collins, and they are hoping his working-class bona fides will hold down her margins in the reddest parts of the state — which could push Democrats to elevate similar candidates elsewhere.

“He is a true working-class champion — he’s not an academic that’s stepped in, or a political operative,” said Joseph Geevarghese, the executive director of Our Revolution, a progressive group that emerged from Senator Bernie Sanders’s first presidential campaign (which Jackson worked on in 2016).

Jackson’s candidacy, Geevarghese said, will be an “example and case study in how our movement succeeds or fails going forward.”

Jackson’s general-election campaign, which is only officially two days old, is leaning heavily on his biography. A fifth-generation logger from the tiny town of Allagash, Maine, he joined a 1998 blockade of the northern border to stop cheap Canadian labor from going in and American wood from going out.

“The people that I worked beside were getting screwed, and no one in power seemed to care about that,” Jackson said on Saturday, explaining the origins of the populism that would take him first to the State House — where he was elected in 2002 as an independent — and then to the State Senate, where he served as president.

“We’re not from the left, we’re not from the right,” Jackson said before some of the delegates piped up to join him. “We’re from the bottom, and we are rising.”

Jackson is, of course, the second man with a working-class persona Democrats have turned to this year to take down Collins. The party’s primary voters decisively rejected Gov. Janet Mills, a former prosecutor and the choice of the party establishment (and, as she frequently pointed out, the only Democrat who has actually won a statewide election since 2006).

Democrats are quick to say that Jackson’s politics and life story make him an obvious inheritor of Platner’s insurgent movement. What they don’t say out loud is that someone who actually worked as a logger might be a better avatar than Platner, a prep-school alum and gentleman oyster farmer whose working-class credentials were open to debate but who seized on a wave of populist anger anyway.

“We need people like loggers, millwrights, papermakers, ditch diggers — anybody in there that can represent us because they are us,” Joel Hooper, 63, a Democrat and former millwright who lost his job when the mill where he worked closed down, told me on Saturday, shortly after voting to make Jackson the new nominee.

“We’re trying,” he added, “to make this party represent the working class again.”

Jackson is one of several Democratic candidates around the country who are leaning on hardscrabble personal stories to make inroads with working-class voters who have peeled off from the party in the Trump era.

Some Democrats have done that successfully. Take Representative Jared Golden, who represents northern Maine, including the turf Jackson represented as a state lawmaker, or Representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington State, who owns an auto shop.

But it doesn’t always work. Remember when Democrats hoped that Gov. Tim Walz of Minnesota, with his camo hats and working knowledge of a car engine, would help former Vice President Kamala Harris win over white men?

“This is the category error that the left is making,” Matt Bennett, a co-founder of the centrist think tank Third Way, told me, “which is, if you find someone that looks the part, that they will be satisfied with that.”

Republicans are moving to tie Jackson to Platner and present him as too far left for Maine, hoping to neutralize any cultural affinity he might have with voters in the rural and conservative areas of the state.

Democrats are talking little about the 20 years he spent in state government. And they are hoping that his life story is enough to paper over the obvious weaknesses of his candidacy, including his stark fund-raising disadvantage; his halting speaking style; and the reports, including some from my colleagues, that he was quick to anger during his time in state government.

“If there aren’t more stories that we don’t know, I think that’s just who Troy has always been,” said Representative Chellie Pingree, a Democrat. “I guess without thoroughly excusing anybody’s anger, people are so frustrated. They are looking for candidates who show their passion and do a little fist pounding.”

item.title: Hiker Trekked 10 Miles to Safety After Impaling Himself on Pole
item.description:
David Cifaldi and two of his friends had been hiking for about seven hours up Montana’s tallest mountain on July 20 when he slipped on a rock and fell. He saw one of his trekking poles on the ground, but the second one was nowhere to be found.

Then he rolled over. Something wasn’t right.

“Oh,” he recalled. “This thing is sticking out of me.”

Mr. Cifaldi, 32, had impaled himself on the pole. He immediately went into nurse mode: Mr. Cifaldi is a wound nurse at St. Vincent Regional Hospital in Billings, Mont.

The pole was jutting at an angle into his left latissimus dorsi muscle, below his armpit, and out through his back. He wasn’t in pain, there was no blood, he was able to take deep breaths and could feel the trekking pole through his skin. He was two to three miles from the summit of Granite Peak, elevation of about 12,800 feet.

The three friends had started their ascent at 2 a.m. with plans to camp overnight at Froze-to-Death Plateau and then summit the mountain. Mr. Cifaldi had made it to the plateau a number of times, but never to the summit. His friend Jesse Ross, who had reached the top successfully, was leading Mr. Cifaldi and another friend, Brad Reich, up the mountain.

They made it to the plateau by sunrise.

“As you get up there, you feel like you’re in, like, ‘The Lord of the Rings,’ or something like that,” Mr. Cifaldi said in an interview on Monday. “It’s just mountains and green.”

Everyone was cruising at that point. The weather was perfect — mid-60s and sunny, no wind — and the summit was in reach. Then Mr. Cifaldi lost his footing.

While one friend sent an SOS signal on a GPS phone, the other took pictures of the wound so Mr. Cifaldi could assess it.

“I was pretty confident it was not in my chest or lung,” he said.

Hoping to avoid an expensive lift off the mountain via helicopter, he walked around and found he wasn’t lightheaded and told his friends, “I think we can get out of here.”

And so they went.

With search and rescue on standby, the three friends slowly made their way down the mountain, taking about six hours to reach the trailhead at Mystic Lake. Mr. Ross went ahead, warning any hikers that Mr. Cifaldi was coming down the trail with a “gnarly” looking injury but assuring them that he was otherwise OK. Mr. Reich was close behind monitoring the puncture after Mr. Cifaldi gave him a crash course in emergency medicine.

They crossed boulder fields and stretches of snow, taking breaks every so often. By 3:30 p.m., after trekking about 10 miles, Mr. Cifaldi was in an ambulance on his way to the nearest hospital.

Even injured, Mr. Cifaldi felt safe: He had two “rock-solid friends” who never wavered once, he said. He knew he was going to be OK when they stopped about halfway down for a snack and “started making shish kebab jokes,” Mr. Cifaldi said. “By the end, they were calling me ‘Bob’ on the way out.”

By the time Mr. Cifaldi reached a small hospital near the mountain, the pole had been inside him for seven hours. He begged a nurse practitioner to take it out, but she told him, “If you bleed, I can’t help you.”

So they transferred him to a hospital he knew well — his own. He refused an ambulance and had his friends drive him there.

When he arrived in the emergency room, Mr. Cifaldi said, he was “a very popular guy.” They got to work on him quickly, taking X-rays and running blood tests. His doctors wanted to book him for surgery, but with another trauma case ahead of him, it would be a two-hour wait.

“At that point I was fed up,” he recalled. “I was, like, please somebody just take this thing out of me.”

So the doctors induced conscious sedation, in which the patient is anesthetized yet awake, and pulled the pole out. As they removed it, doctors inserted a tube to drain the area.

“When I came back to, that was the first time I had pain,” Mr. Cifaldi said. He was adamant about returning to work the next day, but doctors ordered him to rest for a week.

Mr. Cifaldi returned to work on Monday, a little sore, a little tired, but grateful. He talked to a therapist about the accident to help him process it all. Three centimeters further in “and I’d be dead, or at least in grave peril,” he said.

His biggest takeaway from the ordeal: Have a way to contact emergency services.

“I’m not an amateur hiker. I’m fit and active,” he said. “I was training to run a marathon when this all happened. And it was just a freak accident.” Having a way to reach out to a search-and-rescue team “made all the difference in the world.”

In addition to being sore, Mr. Cifaldi feels badly that his friends didn’t make it to the summit.

“We were going make it, 100 percent, there was no doubt. Everything was perfect,” he said. “I’m hoping next year I’ll be able to say, hey, I went back and I did it.”

item.title: Trump Backs New Iran Talks but It’s Unclear What He Hopes to Achieve This Time
item.description:
President Trump said on Monday that there was “a good chance” a new round of diplomacy with Iran could yield a breakthrough, but warned that he would quickly resume the airstrikes he paused over the weekend if that did not happen.

“We’re talking right now,” Mr. Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One. “Iran took a beating over the last 14 days, and they asked us very nicely, ‘please stop, let’s meet,’” he said, an assertion that Iran quickly denied.

Having failed to achieve his goals through two weeks of renewed attacks on Iran, it is unclear whether Mr. Trump can expect better results through more negotiations, including on his crucial objective of restoring free navigation to the Strait of Hormuz.

Former U.S. officials said that a defiant Iran probably sees Mr. Trump’s leverage waning fast as the November midterm elections approach. Some top Republican officials are already urging him to finish the conflict.

Yet Mr. Trump will face a crosswind on Tuesday when Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel visits the White House. Mr. Netanyahu favors continuing the war and is likely to make that case to Mr. Trump, analysts said.

While Mr. Trump insisted that the recent U.S. attacks had led Iran to request new talks with his administration, Iran denied that claim and gave no sign that it was prepared to make new concessions or even speak directly with American officials.

And Saudi Arabia said it had intercepted several drones launched by Iranian-backed Iraqi militias on Monday despite the U.S. bombing pause. Other countries in the region, including Israel and Jordan, also reported drone attacks.

During a news conference on Monday, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman, Esmail Baghaei, denied that Iran had offered to negotiate in return for a U.S. bombing pause. Tehran will communicate with Washington only through intermediaries, he said.

Qatar and Pakistan have been playing that go-between role. They are trying to restore a June 17 cease-fire agreement between the United States and Iran that collapsed this month. The agreement halted U.S. strikes on Iran, lifted an American naval blockade on Iranian ports, and, in Mr. Trump’s telling, reopened the Strait of Hormuz to free navigation.

But Iran interpreted vague language in the cease-fire deal as granting it authority over the strait. Iranian officials insisted that ships follow a designated route along its coastline and attacked some tankers that took an alternate route along Oman’s coast.

By early July most shipping through the waterway had ground to a halt. Oil prices shot back above $100 for the first time in weeks.

In response, Mr. Trump restored the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports and resumed airstrikes.

Mr. Trump warned last week that he might dramatically escalate his attacks on Iran. He threatened to hit major infrastructure targets like bridges and power plants, along with an underground facility known as Pickaxe Mountain that experts fear Iran might use to reconstitute its nuclear program. He decided against that approach over the weekend after warnings from senior officials that the United States was running low on antimissile interceptors and other critical munitions.

Mr. Trump denied on Monday that the U.S. military was running low on such weapons. “We have a lot of ammunition,” he said, while perhaps hinting at a more complicated truth: “I’d like to have more, to be honest, but so much was given to Ukraine.”

Mr. Trump insisted that greater military pressure had brought Iran back to talks, without providing details about what sort of diplomacy was underway. “The only reason they want to meet is because we’ve been hitting them very hard,” he said.

Iran has also been engaged in talks with Oman about the management of the Strait of Hormuz, which runs through the territorial waters of both countries. (The United Nations considers the strait an international waterway that cannot be subject to the sort of fees and tolls on commercial shipping that Iran has sought to impose since the war began.)

Omani diplomats visited Tehran for talks on Friday and Saturday, an Iranian foreign ministry spokesman told reporters on Sunday.

Michael Makovsky, the president and CEO of the Jewish Institute for National Security of America, a hawkish pro-Israel think tank based in Washington, said that Mr. Netanyahu will urge Mr. Trump to resume a major military campaign against Iran. He added that Mr. Netanyahu, who played a key role in persuading Mr. Trump to launch the war, will be sensitive to perceptions that he is pressuring the U.S. president.

Mr. Makovsky said he hoped Mr. Trump chose a return to military action. “Almost four months of diplomacy has gone nowhere,” he said, adding that “the war-diplomacy stop-and-starts make us look fickle and weak.”

But as Mr. Trump learned over the past two weeks of escalation, military action tends to rattle markets and send energy prices soaring, hitting American consumers hard at the gas pump.

High U.S. gas prices are already stressing congressional Republicans ahead of the midterm elections, and signs of their impatience about the conflict are growing: “We got to wrap it up,” Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters last week.

“The Iranians know that Trump’s timelines are shorter than their own timelines,” said Dana Stroul, the Pentagon’s top Middle East policy official in the Biden administration.

Ms. Stroul argued that Mr. Trump would need more help from U.S. allies to solve his dilemma.

One sign of that came Monday with word that U.S. and British officials are planning to convene a high-level meeting in London this week to discuss a potential international coalition to protect shipping in the strait.

Details of the meeting were still being worked out, including whether Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, would attend, and what the goals of the gathering would be.

But a senior Defense Department official, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss diplomatic matters, said the meeting had taken on greater significance after the latest wave of U.S. attacks against Iranian military sites failed to stymie Iran’s attacks on commercial ships in the strait.

Another U.S. military official added on Monday that Iran was continuing to harass ships seeking to transit the strait.

“The Trump administration tried going it alone against Iran, and now they are actually waking up to the fact that working with allies and partners in an international construct is absolutely necessary if they want to restore freedom of navigation,” said Ms. Stroul, who is director of research at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.

Some Western European countries have previously said they would send ships to help patrol the strait, but with a major caveat: The hostilities between Iran and the United States must end first.

Helene Cooper and Eric Schmitt contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: AIPAC Attacks and an ‘Ogre’ Jab: 6 Takeaways From Michigan’s Senate Debate
item.description:
A week before Michigan’s primary contest for Senate, the two Democrats seeking the nomination spent much of their final debate hitting out at each other over campaign finance and who would focus more on helping their state.

Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive former public health official, repeatedly accused Representative Haley Stevens, a moderate, of being a tool of corporate interests. She declared that he would use the Senate as a steppingstone to political celebrity and would not put the needs of their state first.

Their ideological and stylistic divide, starkly illuminated in the debate on Monday and in the final weeks of the campaign, is as broad as any in a major primary campaign this year. The Michigan seat is seen as crucial in the race for Senate control. The winner of the Democratic primary will face former Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican, in the general election in a race to succeed Senator Gary Peters, a Democrat who is retiring.

On Monday, the candidates’ divergent visions presented Michigan Democrats with a stark choice: Do they want a senator who will work with Democratic leaders in Washington and occupy a middle lane? Or one who will push for progressive causes like “Medicare for all” and ending U.S. aid to Israel?

Here are six takeaways from the debate:

The Senate primary in Michigan has become the showpiece fight between Democrats who want to fundamentally alter the nation’s relationship with Israel by cutting U.S. military aid and those who back continued American support for the Jewish state.

It has also become a central battle over money in politics. The main super PAC for the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the nation’s leading pro-Israel group, has so far spent $30.6 million on advertising backing Ms. Stevens, according to data from AdImpact, a media tracking firm. Six other super PACs that have not disclosed their donors have spent a collective $29.4 million on her behalf.

Throughout the hourlong debate, Dr. El-Sayed reminded viewers that Ms. Stevens was heavily backed by super PAC money. He argued that it would influence her conduct in the Senate.

“Just last week, our friend here voted to send 3.3 billion of your tax dollars to a foreign government,” he said, referring to Ms. Stevens’s House vote against cutting off U.S. aid to Israel. “That is the pro quo that comes with the quid of $30 million spent by AIPAC.”

Ms. Stevens, as she has throughout the campaign, did not engage with questions about AIPAC support. She declared herself “transparent” and sought to pivot to “the affordability crisis here in Michigan.”

There is little doubt that Dr. El-Sayed is a smoother talker than Ms. Stevens. While she sometimes meandered through thoughts and injected buzzwords into her debate responses, he spoke in the smooth cadence of a veteran podcaster — a role she attacked him for once having.

“My opponent here, Abdul, he is such a talented guy,” Ms. Stevens said. “He’s written three books, he’s had 300 podcasts. You know, he’s had all this attention, but the deal is, is we don’t need a celebrity candidate. We don’t need a celebrity senator. We need somebody who is committed to six years of hard, unglamorous work.”

At one point, she accused Dr. El-Sayed of using the Senate race as a way station en route to running for president. And indeed, he has articulated big ambitions about changing the Democratic Party from a perch in the Senate, starting with the party’s relationship with Israel.

Dr. El-Sayed is not a democratic socialist, and he is not endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America. And yet the debate’s moderator asked him about accusations that he was a socialist — “not that that’s a bad word.”

Dr. El-Sayed parried the question and said that a larger threat than socialism was capitalism run amok, dominated by corporate monopolies and oligarchs.

“I’m not a socialist,” he said. “I’m just a capitalist who understands how capitalism works.”

Much of the debate was conducted on Dr. El-Sayed’s terms. Discussion about AIPAC-tied funding and U.S. support for Israel left Ms. Stevens defending positions that have become broadly unpopular among Democratic primary voters.

When it came to an exchange about Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Ms. Stevens spoke about her efforts — which were ultimately futile — to redirect funding for the agency that Republicans in Congress had approved.

Dr. El-Sayed’s message was more unequivocal. He would abolish ICE altogether — and he thought more Democrats should praise immigration in general.

“We need Democrats who are going to stand up and actually talk about the great good that immigration has done for our country in the first place,” said Dr. El-Sayed, whose parents immigrated to Michigan from Egypt. “The idea that somehow we can’t say ‘abolish ICE’ because we’re so afraid of what they’re going to say, when we’ve seen ICE terrorize people in our streets, to me, it is exactly the kind of cowardice that we don’t need from Democrats.”

Ms. Stevens is counting on Black voters in Michigan to carry her to victory in the primary. Polls show her leading among them, and AIPAC-tied advertising features footage of former President Barack Obama praising Ms. Stevens at a rally when she first ran for Congress in 2018.

Throughout the debate on Monday, she sought to emphasize her connection with and appeal to Black voters.

She slipped a reference to her support for “equity and inclusion” into a response to a question about a recent rally that Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York held in Michigan for Dr. El-Sayed. And she sought to dismiss Dr. El-Sayed’s populist appeal and large crowds by suggesting that she was spending her campaign time — which has included far fewer advertised public events — dropping in to speak with Black business owners.

“I know it’s great to hold, host rallies and have these fun events,” she said. “But everywhere I have gone in Michigan, I have taken the time to visit a minority-owned business.”

In the final weeks of the primary, as some of Dr. El-Sayed’s online supporters mocked Ms. Stevens for her accent and her speech patterns, he made a plea for kindness in the campaign.

But his own colorful language in a leaked audio recording reported by Politico, in which he suggested that if “you put one ogre on a pike, and then everyone else gets the message,” briefly put him on the defensive during the debate. Dr. El-Sayed said that he had been speaking about a primary challenge to Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, the towering Democrat whose politics have swerved to the right.

Ms. Stevens responded by reciting Dr. El-Sayed’s attacks against Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and former Senator Debbie Stabenow, who have both endorsed her. When Dr. El-Sayed then suggested that the debate should be less about their personalities and more about their politics, Ms. Stevens offered a mocking appreciation for his clarification.

“Well, thank you,” she said, “for clarifying that you didn’t call me an ogre.”

item.title: Fauci, in Private Diary, Reflected on Covid’s Origins and His Own Fame
item.description:
The world was just awakening to the novel coronavirus, and a full-fledged pandemic was still in the future, when Dr. Anthony S. Fauci jotted a note in his diary on Jan. 26, 2020, musing about whether the virus might have originated in an open-air “wet market,” where live animals were sold, in Wuhan, China.

“Now we know the market was not the source, it was the amplifier,” Dr. Fauci, then the government’s top infectious disease expert, wrote. “Having said that, somewhere the virus jumped from animals to humans.”

Those private reflections became public this past weekend when Senator Rand Paul, Republican of Kentucky, released more than 1,100 pages of Dr. Fauci’s typewritten daily notes as part of his investigation into whether the virus might have leaked from a laboratory and whether, as Mr. Paul claims, Dr. Fauci lied to Congress about it.

The diary does not provide the smoking gun the senator is seeking. Rather, it echoes past disclosures showing Dr. Fauci wrestling with a fast-moving crisis as scientists’ views evolved. But it further inflames a polarizing political battle over the origins of the virus and how history should treat Dr. Fauci.

It also paints a portrait of Dr. Fauci as obsessed with himself, reveling in his own importance and the celebrities he knows, from the actress Julia Roberts to the singers Joan Baez and Barbra Streisand. It shows, as well, the pressure he was under, as he became the public face of the government’s response while at the same time countering what he called “slanderous lies” about him spread by “extreme right elements in society.”

On Wednesday, Dr. Fauci is scheduled to testify under subpoena before the Senate Homeland Security Committee, which Mr. Paul chairs. Although Dr. Fauci received a “pre-emptive pardon” from former President Joseph R. Biden Jr., Mr. Paul has repeatedly referred him to the Justice Department for criminal prosecution.

“What he wrote privately and what he told the country are two different stories,” the senator wrote on the social media platform X.

Senator Paul’s office did not respond to requests for comment about how he obtained the diary. But it is typewritten, suggesting Dr. Fauci may have taken notes on his work computer, possibly for his memoir, published in 2024.

Dr. Fauci declined comment.

The debate over whether Covid-19 leaked from a lab, either accidentally or intentionally, has raged for years. Some Republicans fixated on it after President Trump floated the idea in the early months of the pandemic in his first term. Democrats rejected the theory, insisting that Mr. Trump was trying to blame China while distracting attention from his administration’s failings in containing Covid’s spread.

Dr. Fauci has long maintained that he is open to the idea of a lab leak, but believes the virus was natural in origin.

Much of the public discussion has centered on the question of whether the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, which Dr. Fauci led for nearly 40 years, had funded so-called “gain-of-function” research at a laboratory in Wuhan, China.

“Gain-of-function” research, which Dr. Fauci referred to in his diary as “GOF,” involves tinkering with the genetic makeup of viruses to better understand how they evolve — and to prevent against future pandemics. It is strictly regulated by the government. Dr. Fauci has repeatedly insisted that his institute did not fund such research in China, and Mr. Paul has insisted that he did.

“If anybody is lying here, senator, it is you,” Dr. Fauci said in response to questions from Mr. Paul in July 2021.

At the outset of the pandemic, the public health establishment dismissed the idea of a lab leak as a “conspiracy theory.” Dr. Fauci wrote as much on Jan. 31, 2020: “There have been conspiracy theories that the virus was given GOF by inserted mutations and deliberately or accidentally released in Wuhan.”

But the diary, echoing previously released emails, reflects that Dr. Fauci was uncertain.

When a respected scientist expressed concerns that the virus might have indeed been engineered, Dr. Fauci convened a conference call with leading virologists and evolutionary biologists who debated the idea. In the emails, Dr. Fauci had said that if their suspicions bore out, the scientists would have to alert “appropriate authorities,” including the F.B.I.

“There was not total agreement” on the call, Dr. Fauci wrote in the diary. Of 11 scientists, not including Dr. Fauci, just two were convinced that the virus emerged naturally. The others were not sure. Dr. Fauci did not state his own view.

Mr. Paul pointed to the entry as an indication that the scientific establishment was more divided than Dr. Fauci let on. He also seized on Dr. Fauci’s January 2020 “amplifier” comment as evidence of dishonesty. But Dr. Fauci had made the same comment three weeks later in an interview with U.S.A. Today.

Dr. Fauci, 85, who retired from government service at the end of 2022, has long maintained a public profile. He has advised seven presidents, on matters ranging from AIDS to anthrax and Ebola, and has been a familiar figure in Washington circles, showing up at events like the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner.

But the pandemic catapulted him into new territory, as he himself notes.

“It is not hyperbole to say that today I am the most famous and talked about person in the country and one of the most recognizable” in the world, he wrote after a “very flattering” front-page story in The Washington Post.

The entries were also full of references to Hollywood stars, some of whom seemed star-struck over him.

Barbra Streisand called asking for vaccine advice. When Dr. Fauci told her he listened to her music on Alexa, the virtual assistant, she confessed she didn’t know what Alexa was. “I accidentally butt called her later in the evening,” Dr. Fauci wrote, and when he played her music over Alexa, she “absolutely loved it!”

Joan Baez painted a portrait of him. Julia Roberts introduced him at an awards ceremony.

“She is so charming, natural, fun and amazingly beautiful,” Dr. Fauci wrote of Ms. Roberts. “When my image came up on the screen,” he added, “she gasped and said that every time she sees me her throat gets dry and she gets nervous.”

Senator Paul taunted Dr. Fauci on social media about the disclosures, writing that “While America buried loved ones, Anthony Fauci was counting headlines that doted over him.” He posted what appeared to be an A.I.-generated image of Dr. Fauci, dressed in a bright sweater and lying on a pink blanket, writing in a diary as if he were a teenage girl.

Mr. Paul has been investigating Covid’s origins, and Dr. Fauci, for years.

Some government agencies, including the Department of Energy and the Central Intelligence Agency, now favor the lab leak theory. When President Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, his administration steered the Covid.gov website, used by the Biden administration to promote vaccines, to a new page that blared the words “LAB LEAK: The true origins of Covid-19.”

Last year, the Kentucky senator released some of Dr. Fauci’s emails, including one in which Dr. Fauci asked Dr. Francis Collins, then the director of the National Institutes of Health, to “please delete this email after you read it” — evidence, Mr. Paul has said, that Dr. Fauci was trying to keep information from Congress.

Dr. Fauci’s critics spent much of the past several days digging through the records for tidbits in which he appeared to contradict himself. In a 2022 interview with ABC News, reflecting on his 50 years of public service, Dr. Fauci said he had “nothing to do” with school closures.

But in March 2020, he wrote in his diary that he had “convinced” Mayor Bill de Blasio of New York to close city schools. He said he also spoke to a top aide to Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, who had “decided to close the schools in California as well as the bars and restaurants,” based on Dr. Fauci’s suggestion.

On Monday, Mr. Paul released another 500 pages of Dr. Fauci’s records. These were from 2001, documenting his work with former President George W. Bush to create a program to bring AIDS drugs to Africa.

Mr. Bush later awarded Dr. Fauci the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor. “Those who know Tony do admit one flaw: sometimes he forgets to stop working,” Mr. Bush said during the ceremony. “He regularly puts in 80-hour weeks. And from time to time, he’s even found notes on his windshield left by co-workers that say things like, “Go home.’”

Benjamin Mueller contributed to this report.

item.title: A California Beach City Struggles to Cope With Rowdy Outsiders
item.description:
Earlier this month, dozens of Newport Beach residents lined up at a City Council meeting to deliver the same message: Leaders of the Southern California coastal enclave needed to prevent another fracas like the one that took place on July 4.

Thousands of young people had descended on the beaches of the city’s storied Balboa Peninsula, attracted by posts on TikTok and other social media. Many seemed intent on making trouble. They shot illegal fireworks in all directions, scuffled and even looted an upscale grocery store. More than 300 people were arrested on July 4 alone. Most of them were 25 or younger, and most were from out of state.

The mess was “a predictable consequence of a growing reputation that Newport Beach has become a place where bad behavior is tolerated,” Maureen Cotton, the president of a local community group, told the council members.

City leaders vowed to undertake a broader review of regulations aimed at managing crowds on the beach. At its meeting on Tuesday, the City Council will discuss potential changes, including a youth curfew, expanding the city’s definition of a public nuisance and restricting mass gatherings planned on social media.

The Independence Day rowdiness tapped into national anxieties about social-media-driven “teen takeovers” and other misbehavior by young people.

But it also became the latest front in a long-running debate about who controls one of California’s most precious resources: its coastline.

Similar battles have played out in other beachfront communities across the country, including in Florida’s Panhandle and in New York.

Although residents urged City Council members to consider a wide range of solutions, such as further restricting short-term rentals and holding parents accountable for teens, there was one fix that nearly all of them, including Ms. Cotton, agreed on: “I’d love you to seriously consider limiting vehicle and pedestrian access to the peninsula on the Fourth of July,” she said.

In California, the public’s right of access to the beach is enshrined in the state constitution. But the specific rules governing that access — and how those rules are enforced — are often a point of contention between visitors, coastal property owners and beachside communities.

Beachfront real estate has become increasingly expensive, with Newport Beach homes hitting an average sale price of $3.7 million, according to Zillow. Beach city residents say they pay a premium to live peacefully, with ocean views.

At the same time, Californians who once lived in coastal cities have been moving farther inland to fast-growing suburbs in the Riverside and San Bernardino areas, or even out of state, to cities like Phoenix and Las Vegas. For inland residents, summer treks to the beach are one of few low-cost respites from punishing, dangerous heat.

Alyssa Dominguez, 29, who was sitting under a beach tent looking at the waves on the Balboa Peninsula in early July, said she and her family visited from the Inland Empire every summer. She had seen the dramatic footage of police officers on horseback breaking up crowds of revelers on July 4, and she understood why it would alarm residents.

But she said it would not be fair to cut off access to the peninsula’s beaches on a major holiday simply because one had gone awry.

“It happened once. That doesn’t mean it’s going to keep happening,” she said.

Locals say that summertime crowds have become unsustainable, with roads often so packed that they can barely leave their own homes. The hundreds of thousands of visitors, they say, wreak havoc, leaving trash and throwing materials that shouldn’t be burned into bonfires on the sand.

Leaders of California beach cities have tried to limit parking near the shore, curb gridlock by enforcing Byzantine traffic patterns and crack down on behaviors that they say diminish their quality of life.

In Laguna Beach, just south of Newport Beach, city officials prepare for summer as if they are going to battle. Residents have sought to keep visitors from parking on side streets, prompting clashes over whether those measures also effectively block access to the sand itself. There, and in Malibu farther north, videos on social media last summer showed property owners trying to shoo away beachgoers, drawing outrage.

Legal fights over blocked beach roads are common, such as a decades-long conflict over access to beaches in Hollister Ranch, near Santa Barbara.

Such efforts have often met opposition from the powerful California Coastal Commission, which since 1972 has been tasked with protecting the beach and public access to it.

Newport Beach has been no stranger to such fights. A decade ago, a plan to remove wood-burning fire rings from two of its large beaches spun into a regulatory proxy war over public beach access and air quality protections. Today, Newport Beach has some bonfire rings that burn wood and some that require charcoal.

More recently, in an effort to discourage rowdy behavior, Newport Beach increased fines for drinking on the beach, restricted the size of beach shades and boosted penalties on the owners of short-term rental properties for guest misbehavior. The city also began a public messaging campaign called “Not in Newport” to tell young visitors to take their fake identification cards and illegal fireworks elsewhere.

None of that was enough on July 4. Over the course of the holiday weekend, more than 420,000 people flooded onto the city’s beaches, which have long been party destinations on summer holidays. Police made more than 400 arrests, including the 328 arrests after illegal behavior escalated on July 4 itself.

At the City Council meeting days later, the police chief showed a slide comparing Newport Beach’s response to the social media “takeover” with similar incidents in other cities: In Raleigh, N.C., and in St. Louis, police made dozens of arrests and they also responded to multiple shootings at each gathering, including at least one that was fatal.

“I would like to note there were no shootings, no serious injuries that occurred, no structures burned to the ground,” said Dave Miner, the city’s police chief. “Newport Beach had a very massive law enforcement response.”

The events in Newport Beach were hard to predict, officials said. Mayor Lauren Kleiman said that the authorities had flagged plans for similar unsanctioned gatherings in nearby Huntington Beach and at Knott’s Berry Farm, an Orange County theme park.

Another mass gathering at Newport Beach, planned for Sunday night, was discussed online. The Newport Beach police department deployed 100 officers, including from other departments. But the expected crowd never showed up.

Still, members of the City Council said that they were open to figuring out ways to block or restrict traffic onto the Balboa Peninsula on big holidays.

“We get to be stewards of something that is amazing, but we don’t own it and we don’t control it,” Noah Blom, the mayor pro tem, told residents at the meeting. “If that was the option: put a gate on the Peninsula, or blow the bridge, for my money, I’d be right there.”

Tactics deployed by some beach communities, such as high parking fees and residency requirements in the Hamptons in New York, would be unlikely to pass legal muster in California. Ms. Kleiman said she had reached out to the Coastal Commission to figure out what kind of regulations the city could impose.

Kate Huckelbridge, the commission’s executive director, said in a statement that the agency planned to work closely with the city to help prevent another situation like the July 4 incident. She did not address questions about whether the city would be allowed to restrict beach access.

In Huntington Beach, Mayor Casey McKeon said that closing the city’s beaches would be impossible. Its stretch of the coast is home to wide, sandy beaches, including many with enormous parking lots. Several big roads lead to the coast.

Mr. McKeon said that the city’s police and fire departments were used to large events and were prepared to respond if things got out of hand.

For the most part, everyone gets along fine at the beach.

On the Balboa Peninsula just before the City Council meeting where residents vented their frustrations, it was a typically idyllic summer day. Families played in the fine sand and crystalline blue waters, while people biked along the boardwalk.

Jayden Kelsch, 22, was working the door at Mutt Lynch’s, a popular watering hole, where visitors and locals were gathering to watch a World Cup match and sip from goblets of beer.

He said that while the July 4 incident was tough for business — the bar closed early — he wasn’t afraid. It was, in his view, mostly teens looking for online clout. Still, Mr. Kelsch said he was confident that the city would respond somehow.

“I definitely think that this situation opened the city’s eyes to what these young kids are capable of and the extreme lengths they’ll go to just to make content,” he said.

As someone who's lived in California for most of my life, I've seen this struggle play out many times — trying to protect public beach access while still respecting the real concerns of local residents.

item.title: Senate Democrats Press Blanche on Times Subpoenas
item.description:
Senate Democrats on Monday demanded answers from Todd Blanche, President Trump’s nominee for attorney general, about subpoenas he authorized to New York Times journalists, including whether President Trump had pressured the Justice Department to issue them.

In a letter to Mr. Blanche that came as Republicans are pressing to confirm him, Democrats on the Senate Judiciary Committee argued that federal prosecutors violated internal standards when they issued subpoenas seeking grand jury testimony and phone records from several Times journalists who had reported on the security vulnerabilities of the jet that Qatar gave to Mr. Trump to use as Air Force One.

“The government’s conduct involved a series of bad-faith efforts to conceal notice of these subpoenas and intimidate journalists and their families following the publication of a story that allegedly enraged President Trump,” the Democrats wrote.

The letter raised new questions about the leadership of Mr. Blanche, the acting attorney general, ahead of a planned vote of the Judiciary Committee on Thursday on whether to advance his nomination to the full Senate.

With Democrats unified in opposition, Republicans cannot afford any defections. So far, two Republicans, Senators John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, have said they are undecided about Mr. Blanche, though they have not cited the subpoenas when asked about their concerns.

The Justice Department withdrew the subpoenas last week after a federal judge raised similar questions about whether prosecutors had followed the law and the department’s internal regulations on investigations involving news reporters.

The Democrats asked for a briefing from Justice Department officials on whether prosecutors followed their own rules. They also raised a number of questions about the department’s investigation, including whether Mr. Trump or any White House aides directly ordered the Justice Department to subpoena the reporters. The letter was led by Senator Adam B. Schiff, Democrat of California.

Democrats sent the letter as the Senate proceeded with a vote to lay the groundwork for the confirmation of Jay Clayton, the U.S. attorney in Manhattan who is Mr. Trump’s choice to be the next director of national intelligence. At his confirmation hearing, Mr. Clayton said the subpoenas had been issued according to the department’s regulations, but offered few details.

That same day, Mr. Blanche told the Judiciary Committee that federal prosecutors hoped to ask the reporters who had given them classified information concerning Mr. Trump’s plane. He likened reporters to “material witnesses” to a car crash.

The Democrats took particular issue with that statement, writing in their letter that Mr. Blanche had conflated “constitutionally protected news gathering and source protection” with eyewitness observation.

The government began a leak investigation this month after The Times reported that federal officials had significant concerns about the security of Mr. Trump’s plane.

The Democrats accused the Justice Department of violating its own guidelines for “reasonable and timely notice” for media subpoenas by waiting more than a week to notify The Times that it had issued subpoenas for the phone records.

The letter argued that the subpoenas, which sought phone records dating back to Jan. 1, months before The Times published its articles, violated guidance that subpoenas be issued only for “essential” information.

And it argued that the Justice Department had improperly targeted journalists’ relatives when it issued subpoenas for the phone records of the mother of one reporter and the spouses of two others.

The Times made similar arguments in a motion it filed seeking to quash the subpoenas.

item.title: Longtime Union Leader Prepares to Step Back From a Movement Under Threat
item.description:
Lee Saunders, the president of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, traveled to Alaska in March to meet local union leaders pushing to reinstate a pension system for state employees.

Alaska had closed its public retirement program in 2006, after it ran up a multibillion-dollar shortfall. But 20 years later, state agencies have double-digit vacancy rates, a crisis of public-sector employment that has compromised safety and services.

In April, Alaska’s Legislature passed a bill that would restart the retirement program with bipartisan support, aiming to draw and retain workers. But Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, vetoed it in May.

The failure illustrates a tension that came to define Mr. Saunders’s tenure as head of the country’s largest public employee union. While unions have regained favor with the public, they are facing new opposition from many of the country’s leaders.

A 2025 Gallup poll found that 65 percent of Americans approve of labor unions, up from a low of 48 percent in 2009. Over that same time, though, the percentage of American workers in unions has fallen and the power unions wield has been eroded by courts and legislatures. It is a paradox that “reflects our broken political economy,” said Alexander Hertel-Fernandez, a political scientist at Columbia University.

“Policy choices have weakened our labor movement,” he said.

Few people understand the paradox better than Mr. Saunders, 75, who plans to retire in August after 50 years working for the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, or AFSCME, including 15 years as its leader.

Conservatives have long targeted public-sector unions, which they describe as inefficient, coercive and expensive. Now, some on the American left are also calling public-sector unions barriers to progress and productivity. The so-called abundance agenda, while not explicitly antilabor, has set off debates about whether Democrats need to learn how to say no to unions that throw up barriers to better train service, faster construction, more housing.

People who worked with Mr. Saunders over the years say he instilled two principles into the union, which may help it as it confronts new challenges.

The first is the power that comes from keeping the tent open to a wide range of political beliefs and professions. Under Mr. Saunders, the union has stepped back from what he called “in-your-face” politics and leaned into working conditions and protections, issues that he said bridged a partisan divide while creating a grass-roots base.

“We represent Democrats, Republicans, independents, conservatives, progressives,” Mr. Saunders said during an interview at his office in Washington. “We’ve got to concentrate on the issues that impact on our members and why they voted to be in the union.”

The second principle is that public services are vital to the fabric of the country, and that the workers who provide them should be treated with respect, a legacy of the union’s role in the civil rights movement.

“The values he holds are clear and understandable, about workers having a seat at the table, a voice at work, and that, in exchange for the work that they do, to be treated in a dignified and a fair manner,” said Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, who has known Mr. Saunders since the late 1990s.

Mr. Saunders grew up in Cleveland and joined AFSCME’s staff in 1978 as a labor economist in Washington. In 2010, he was elected secretary-treasurer. Two years later, he won a closely fought election to become the union’s president.

Mr. Saunders took office at a time of crisis for state and municipal workers. The Great Recession had hollowed out municipalities around the country. Tax revenues had plummeted, and states, most of which are legally required to keep a balanced budget, were looking for ways to cut spending.

The downturn “resulted in significant attacks on public workers, our jobs, our benefits, our pay, even what we did,” said Steven Kreisberg, a longtime staff member of the union who retired in 2024.

Republican governors — notably in Wisconsin, where AFSCME was founded — gutted collective bargaining agreements. Conservative donors, think tanks and politicians pushed for privatization of public services, and laws that would hamper public-sector unions. In 2018, the Supreme Court ruled that public-sector unions could not compel employees to pay dues or “fair-share fees” if they did not want to be part of the union.

“There was a thought this could be the end of public-sector unionism,” Mr. Kreisberg said. Instead, it pushed unions to make a case for their relevance.

Mr. Saunders had to manage union leaders who believed the union should not make an effort to serve the workers who did not want to pay dues, even though the union was bound by law to represent nonpaying members in bargaining and other matters.

“I didn’t agree with that,” he said in the interview. “We have to figure out ways not to push them away, but to bring them in.”

Mr. Saunders had to reckon with another internal division after George Floyd’s murder, when a subset of members called for law enforcement groups to be banished from the union.

The American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees is a liberal union, but its political composition can be quite diverse: Its 1.4 million dues-paying members across the country include nurses in Michigan, transportation workers in New York and corrections officers in New Mexico, along with domestic workers, clerks, cops and librarians.

Mr. Saunders thought it would be a mistake to push out the police.

“You’re either going to fight for workers or you aren’t going to fight for workers,” he said. “And your strength comes with the numbers that you have, and the classifications that you represent and people sitting down at that table representing all of those classifications — that’s strength, and that’s power.”

Because Mr. Saunders came up through the union’s Washington headquarters, not a local chapter, his critics worried he might lack the workplace experience to lead the union. What Mr. Saunders did have was an understanding of how to talk to lawmakers and — his supporters say — the credibility to forge deals. Mr. Saunders leveraged his relationships with Democratic leaders to help create the $1.9 trillion stimulus package passed in 2021 as the country emerged from the shock of the Covid-19 pandemic.

Negotiating with officials facing revenue shortages is a tough part of the job, he said, but public-sector workers know better than anybody where inefficiencies and waste lie in government. He said he had no patience for arguments about unions “standing in the way.”

“If people believe that the way that you can solve the economic problems that exist in this country is to attack the benefits and wages of public-sector workers, then they’re living in a planet that I’m not on,” Mr. Saunders said. “Because that’s just not for real.”

Mr. Saunders has picked up on another rising wave of public sentiment that could be more influential in coming elections: broad public anger at big companies and Big Tech.

“I am saying point your finger where I believe the blame lays, and that blame is with people that have a bunch of money, want more money, at the expense of working-class people across the country,” Mr. Saunders said. “We cannot fall for the ‘divide and conquer’ trap that is being developed here.”

item.title: Aide Who Had Affair With Newsom 20 Years Ago Details Her Experience
item.description:
An aide who had an affair with Gavin Newsom more than 20 years ago when he was the mayor of San Francisco has written a detailed account of the relationship, which Vanity Fair published on Tuesday.

The first-person essay by the aide, Ruby Rippey, who was working as Mr. Newsom’s appointments secretary at the time, was published just as he finishes his final year as California governor and lays the groundwork for a possible presidential run in 2028.

Ms. Rippey, 54, has rarely spoken publicly of the affair, but it was the talk of San Francisco in 2007 when Mr. Newsom stood before reporters and a bank of television cameras at City Hall to announce, “Everything you’ve heard and read is true.”

He explained that he’d had an affair with Ms. Rippey, the wife of Alex Tourk, a close friend who was then serving as his re-election campaign manager after previously working as his deputy chief of staff. Mr. Tourk had just told Mr. Newsom he was resigning after learning about the affair from his wife.

In her essay, Ms. Rippey does not use Mr. Newsom’s name, but she describes him as the mayor of San Francisco and a man “often described as Kennedy-esque.” (Vanity Fair mentions his name once, in its summary of the essay below the headline.)

She seems to blame herself for betraying her husband and says that her life spiraled as she drank heavily and used cocaine.

She indicates that she was not coerced but also held Mr. Newsom responsible for holding power and proceeding with the affair anyway. “Power does not need to coerce,” she writes. “It only needs to exist. The responsibility to hold the line belongs to the one who holds it. That didn’t happen.”

She writes that their relationship began in the summer of 2005 and lasted for months, with off-and-on encounters.

“I always go to him — his penthouse in Russian Hill, a private back room at a North Beach bar, the W Hotel in Los Angeles,” Ms. Rippey writes in her essay.

“We meet and we drink. There is sex, but it isn’t the point,” she continues. “The point is proximity — to power, to being chosen.”

Mr. Newsom announced in January 2005 that he was divorcing Kimberly Guilfoyle, a former San Francisco prosecutor who is now President Trump’s ambassador to Greece. But even though he was single, the revelation of his affair with Ms. Rippey shocked San Francisco residents and California political circles because he had a relationship with his subordinate and upended his close friend’s marriage.

By the time the affair became public knowledge in early 2007, Mr. Newsom was dating Jennifer Siebel, now his wife, who caused her own brouhaha by publicly dismissing the affair as “a couple nothing incidents” and by calling Ms. Rippey “the culprit.” Ms. Siebel later apologized for the remarks.

Izzy Gardon, a spokesman for Mr. Newsom, said on Tuesday morning: “The governor acknowledged his role and publicly apologized for his conduct nearly two decades ago when he was still mayor. In the time since, he met his wife, started a family and has focused on serving Californians.”

“He addressed this chapter of his life, including in his memoir, and out of respect for everyone involved, does not have anything further to add,” Mr. Gardon continued.

Ms. Rippey was not immediately available on Tuesday morning for comment. She is being represented by Dini Von Mueffling, a public relations strategist who has also worked with Monica Lewinsky and Kristin Cabot, the woman seen on a “kiss cam” being held by her married boss at a Coldplay concert.

Mr. Tourk did not immediately return a text and email seeking comment. After resigning as Newsom’s campaign manager, he founded Ground Floor Public Affairs and has represented companies that include Anthropic, Lyft and the San Francisco Giants.

Ms. Rippey says in Vanity Fair that she considered writing a memoir after the affair became public, but that Kamala Harris, then the city’s district attorney, advised her to say nothing and take time to gain perspective. “It turns out to be the best advice I receive,” Ms. Rippey writes.

The affair was raised by Mr. Newsom’s opponents during his 2018 run for governor, and at the time Ms. Rippey wrote on Facebook that she did not see it as part of the growing #MeToo movement, because while she was his “subordinate,” she was also a 33-year-old married woman and mother who was “free-thinking.”

In the Vanity Fair essay, she writes that she received a phone call in January from an adviser to Mr. Newsom who let her know that she was mentioned in his new memoir. Mr. Newsom primarily discusses her in two paragraphs, calling their relationship “the stupidest and also briefest of affairs.”

She takes issue with Mr. Newsom’s portrayal in the memoir of how he owned up to his role in the affair. He wrote that he had “come clean” to Mr. Tourk, which she felt mistakenly “gives him credit for something I had already done.”

Ms. Rippey, now 20 years sober, lives in Mill Valley, Calif., just north of San Francisco in Marin County. She writes that she and Mr. Tourk divorced and co-parented their son, who is now an adult. She says it took more than a decade for Mr. Tourk to look her in the eye after the affair, but that they have since become close enough again to consider each other family.

Ms. Rippey has remarried and has an 11-year-old son with her second husband.

item.title: Here Is the Schedule for Lindsey Graham’s Services and Funeral
item.description:
The tributes to Senator Lindsey Graham, who died this month, will last for two days across Washington and his home state, South Carolina.

Dozens of dignitaries, including President Trump and South Carolina leaders, are gathering to honor Mr. Graham’s political and policy legacy.

Here’s what’s happening:

In a sign of Mr. Graham’s stature in the Senate, services began at 10 a.m. in the Capitol Rotunda. Chaplains of the House and Senate offered prayers, and political leaders laid wreathes at his hearse. Senators from both parties attended.

Representative Sheri Biggs, a Republican who represents Mr. Graham’s home in South Carolina, said that the senator “spent his life standing for something larger than himself.”

Senator John Thune of South Dakota, the majority leader, offered an emotional tribute to his close friend, choking up as he concluded, “I look forward to the days when you make us all laugh again.”

Vice President JD Vance, who once served with Mr. Graham in the Senate, closed the public remarks, praising Mr. Graham’s legislative passion and willingness to cut deals no matter how heated arguments may have gotten.

A memorial service will take place later Tuesday at the Washington National Cathedral. Some of Mr. Graham’s staff members will be among those who serve as honorary pallbearers.

President Trump, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel and President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine are among those set to attend, along with other congressional and South Carolina leaders.

Mr. Trump will deliver a tribute at the service, along with Sean Hannity, the Fox News host, and Emillie Boggs Roberts, Mr. Graham’s niece.

Tony Perkins, the president of the conservative Family Research Council; Marjorie Dannenfelser, the president of Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America; and the Rev. Franklin Graham, the evangelical minister, will also deliver readings.

Mr. Graham’s casket will return to South Carolina on Wednesday. At 10:45 a.m., the procession will stop at the State House, where Mr. Graham once served.

There will be a presentation by law enforcement, and a flyover from McEntire Joint National Guard Base at about 11 a.m.

At noon, a service will be held at First Baptist Church of Columbia. Gov. Henry McMaster and Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette are among those expected to attend.

The tributes will conclude in Pickens County, where Mr. Graham’s family will bury him in a private ceremony.

item.title: Anthropic A.I. Model Finds Flaws in Tough-to-Crack Encryption Algorithms
item.description:
A leading A.I. model built by Anthropic has found flaws in a weakened version of a digital encryption standard that is in pervasive use throughout the internet, the company’s researchers said Tuesday, underscoring the potential risks to global cybersecurity posed by ever-improving artificial intelligence software.

During a research-led test, the model, Claude Mythos Preview, was able to detect new ways to attack cryptographic algorithms that keep everything from online bank transactions to private communications to state secrets safe from the prying eyes of hackers or other unwanted third parties.

The research shows that A.I. could one day challenge core assumptions for how the internet operates. While experts say A.I. is likely to upend many industries, A.I. systems have made particularly rapid advancements in coding and cybersecurity.

The flaws identified do not concern a cryptographic standard currently in use today, which means that modern banking and communication systems are not subject to immediate potential intrusions from A.I. Instead, Anthropic’s technology cracked a watered-down version of an algorithm for Advanced Encryption Standard, or A.E.S., a ubiquitous protocol that safeguards web traffic, wireless networks, data storage and more.

It is common to perform tests on weaker versions of encryption algorithms to understand whether more powerful computers could someday crack the actual standards, akin to solving a simpler math problem to identify whether patterns may exist for a more complicated one. In the testing, Mythos was able to break the weaker version of Advanced Encryption Standard in a way that Anthropic said made an assault 200 to 1,000 times faster than what previous human research had managed to do.

While the immediate ramifications are minimal, the long-term implications could be significant. In previous tests, large-language models seemingly could not match or best what humans can do in the mathematically dense field of cryptographic research, but their rapid advances could suggest a future in which top models can surmount traditional internet security protections that are foundational to just about everything that takes place on the internet.

Nicholas Carlini, a research scientist at Anthropic who worked on the cryptography tests, said that tests he was building last year with A.I. models were not nearly as powerful as they are today.

“They could not do problems that I could do when I was 16,” Mr. Carlini, who previously worked at Google’s A.I. division, said in an interview. “Now they are doing state-of-the-art research not previously discovered in the field.”

The latest releases of frontier A.I. models have in recent months spooked governments worldwide, including the Trump administration, with their powerful capabilities, particularly in the field of cybersecurity.

When Mythos first made its debut in April, it was so adept at finding and exploiting computer bugs that Anthropic limited its release to select government agencies and organizations to prevent the possibility of a global digital catastrophe. The Trump administration, which initially once took a hands-off approach to A.I. regulation, has veered toward an ad hoc system of oversight. Many American A.I. companies are now submitting models for review by the government before releasing them publicly, and Mythos remains unavailable to the general public today.

Last week, concerns about the powers of leading A.I. systems peaked again. OpenAI acknowledged its models had leaped out of a safe testing environment, known as a sandbox, that is designed to be unconnected to the internet and successfully hacked into an A.I. technology digital library in an effort to essentially steal the answers to an exam that was grading their abilities.

U.S. and Western intelligence officials have warned for decades that if existing encryption standards were ever broken, it would have profound consequences for digital privacy and national security. China is believed to have collected vast troves of encrypted data, for example, potentially in hopes that it may be able to someday decode the information. The race between the United States and China to build advanced quantum computers that could one day break modern encryption protocols has only heightened concerns around existing standards.

In addition to the attack on the encryption standard, Mythos also orchestrated another improved attack against a different digital cryptographic system known as HAWK that is designed to be bulletproof against both traditional and quantum computers. HAWK is not currently in use, but under consideration by the National Institute of Standards and Technology to become a new standard. The HAWK attack was validated by its authors, and independent cryptographers reviewed the Advanced Encryption Standard attack, Anthropic said, adding that it had shared its findings with the U.S. government and industry partners ahead of publication.

Mythos devised the cryptographic attack on A.E.S. almost entirely autonomously, Anthropic said, but only after first refusing to contemplate the problem because it believed it was impossible to improve on existing methods of analysis. But after some coaxing, the chatbot sat with the puzzle for about a week before engineering its novel attack. Two human researchers then worked for nearly a month to verify that the method appeared correct.

Encryption is foundational to virtually everything that takes place on the internet, and some of the techniques in use today have protected the world’s secrets since the 1970s. Quantum cryptography, which builds on the complicated properties of quantum physics, is a form of encryption that is in theory unbreakable.

Advanced Encryption Standard, or A.E.S., was adopted as a government standard in 2001 and was widely seen as nearly unbreakable at the time. Conventional methods of brute-force code cracking, in which a computer uses trial and error to guess combinations of a password or encryption key, are generally seen as incapable of defeating A.E.S. The standard is believed to have nearly as many key combinations as there are atoms in the observable universe.

But advances in A.I. on some fronts have outpaced what many evangelists assumed was possible even a few years ago. The recent advances have fueled concerns that the mathematical core of internet security standards could one day be vulnerable regardless of advances in quantum computing.

“Given that we are constantly underestimating the power and time of availability of future models, are we really comfortable that two years from now strong encryption won’t be threatened?” said Glenn S. Gerstell, the former general counsel at the National Security Agency.

“Mathematicians would tell you that it shouldn’t be possible given current computing powers to break strong encryption in any meaningful time,” added Mr. Gerstell, who helped write a report on cryptology in 2022. “But I don’t think the capabilities of future models in the medium term — before quantum computing or quantum-proof cryptography — should be dismissed as trivial in this context.”

item.title: Florida Executes One Man, and Plans a 2nd Execution Tonight
item.description:
Florida executed a former police officer on Tuesday and planned to put a second man to death hours later, part of a dramatic rise in carrying out capital punishments during Gov. Ron DeSantis’s second term.

The ex-officer, James Duckett, 68, who had been convicted of sexually assaulting and strangling an 11-year-old girl, was killed by lethal injection at 1:19 p.m. after the Supreme Court declined to stay his sentence.

The second man is scheduled to be killed at 6 p.m., also by injection, which would result in the rare instance of a state carrying out two executions in one day. The man, Dominick Occhicone Jr., is 80, and would be only the second octogenarian put to death in the United States in the last 50 years.

The executions are the 11th and potential 12th in Florida this year, at a time when the Trump administration has encouraged states to more aggressively pursue the death penalty.

Florida has accounted for more than half of the executions in the United States this year, and at least one more is scheduled.

Mr. Duckett was convicted of sexually assaulting and strangling the 11-year-old girl after putting her in his squad car. Mr. Occhicone, the man to be executed later on Tuesday, was convicted of murdering his ex-girlfriend’s parents in 1986.

States have executed multiple people on the same day 11 times since the death penalty was reinstated by a Supreme Court ruling in 1976, according to the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center, which tracks executions. The most recent was in Arkansas, in 2017.

Florida has not done so since killing two men with the electric chair in 1964.

State officials moved ahead with the executions on Tuesday after the Supreme Court denied last-minute requests from both men. No reasoning was given for the denials, and no separate writings or public dissents were noted.

The state is carrying out both executions at Florida State Prison in north-central Florida.

The number of annual executions in the United States has fallen since its peak in 1999, but nearly doubled between 2024 and 2025, driven in large part by Florida’s accelerated pace.

David Ovalle and Abbie VanSickle contributed reporting.

item.title: Graham Mourns Her Brother as She Seeks His Seat
item.description:
Beneath the Capitol dome, Senator Darline Graham stood behind her older brother’s casket stoically on Tuesday as his colleagues in Washington paid tribute to the South Carolina Republican.

For the late Senator Lindsey Graham, who died this month at 71 having never married, his sister was the closest thing to a political spouse that he had. So as world leaders and politicians gathered in Washington to honor him, all eyes were on a somber Ms. Graham, grieving publicly as she juggled her new roles as her brother’s interim replacement and a candidate in a crowded Republican primary to succeed him.

Ms. Graham maintained her composure as officials memorialized Mr. Graham, occasionally dabbing her eyes with a tissue while his Republican colleagues shared stories of the longtime U.S. senator’s larger-than-life personality.

It wasn’t until Ms. Graham approached her brother’s casket in the Capitol Rotunda that tears appeared to trickle down her cheeks.

Ms. Graham placed her palm on the coffin draped with an American flag, her eyes welling up as she reached out to touch it.

Ms. Graham, who was tapped by Gov. Henry McMaster days after her brother’s death to serve as the interim Republican South Carolina senator, now has President Trump’s endorsement in the race to succeed him in the Senate. Mr. Graham died suddenly this month from what officials have preliminarily said was a tear in his aorta.

She has told friends that she was campaigning for the job not because of personal ambition, but rather a desire to honor Mr. Graham, who became her legal guardian as a child after their parents died.

Still, Tuesday’s back-to-back events on Capitol Hill and at the National Cathedral honoring the late senator reflected the reality that Ms. Graham faces as she holds public office for the first time and dives headlong into the crowded race for his seat, all while mourning her brother’s sudden death.

As Vice President JD Vance and other Republicans eulogized Mr. Graham at the Capitol, they at times spoke directly to his sister, who had been his frequent companion at public gatherings during his long political career.

Senator John Thune, Republican of South Dakota and the majority leader, gave condolences to Ms. Graham and her family before he turned toward the coffin and said, through tears, “I look forward to the days when you make us all laugh again.”

In a prayer for the Graham family, Representative Sheri Biggs, Republican of South Carolina, asked that “God continue to show each of us grace that we do not deserve.”

As Ms. Biggs left the podium, Ms. Graham grabbed a cross pendant dangling from her necklace and nodded.

Mr. Graham’s sudden death has set in motion a rapid primary to succeed him, in which Ms. Graham is one of nine Republicans vying for their party’s nomination.

In the interim, Ms. Graham was appointed to fill Mr. Graham’s seat through the remainder of his term ending in January.

On Tuesday, Ms. Graham listened to stories of Mr. Graham’s legacy on Capitol Hill, where he had a reputation for being a skilled debater, a backroom negotiator and a wisecracking character.

“He could be the person you argued with and fought with in one minute, but behind the scenes, without collecting an ounce of credit, he was working for you,” Mr. Vance said.

Ms. Graham looked up at the vice president and smiled slightly, and then turned to the casket and appeared to sigh.
